source: Adding Electric Forces
The net force on a charge is the vector sum of the forces from each of the other charges.
Students add the sizes of forces that point in different directions.

With three or more charges, each pair still obeys Coulomb's law, and the force from one charge does not change because others are nearby. So the net force is the sum of the separate forces, added as vectors, the way you learned in Adding Vectors by Components.

This is the superposition principle, and it is an experimental fact: the force between two charges is the same whether or not other charges are around. So you can find each force on its own and then add. Forces are vectors, so they add tip to tail. On a line, that means adding with signs; at an angle, it means adding components.

$\vec F_{\text{net}} = \vec F_1 + \vec F_2 + \cdots$, each from Coulomb's law. Find each force's size, decide its direction (toward or away from the charge that makes it), then add components: $F_x = \sum F_{ix}$, $F_y = \sum F_{iy}$, $F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2}$.
Two perpendicular forces of 3 and 4 units make a net force of 5, not 7.
The three charges of the first example below. The middle charge is pulled toward both of its neighbors, so the two forces on it partly cancel.
Worked examples
Charges on the $x$-axis: A $= +2.0\,\mu\text{C}$ at $x = 0$, B $= -3.0\,\mu\text{C}$ at $x = 0.20\,\text{m}$, C $= +4.0\,\mu\text{C}$ at $x = 0.50\,\text{m}$. Find the net force on B.
Three in a row
$0.15\,\text{N}$ in the $-x$ direction
From A ($0.20\,\text{m}$ away): $(8.99 \times 10^{9})\dfrac{(2.0 \times 10^{-6})(3.0 \times 10^{-6})}{(0.20)^2} = 1.35\,\text{N}$. Opposite signs attract, so B is pulled toward A: $-1.35\,\text{N}$.
Net: $-1.35 + 1.20 = -0.15\,\text{N}$, so $0.15\,\text{N}$ toward A (to the left).

A $+2.0\,\mu\text{C}$ charge is at the origin, a $+3.0\,\mu\text{C}$ charge at $(0.30\,\text{m}, 0)$ and a $+4.0\,\mu\text{C}$ charge at $(0, 0.40\,\text{m})$. Find the net force on the charge at the origin.
At a right angle
$0.749\,\text{N}$, $36.9^\circ$ below the $-x$ direction
From the charge on the $x$-axis: $$F_1 = (8.99 \times 10^{9})\dfrac{(3.0 \times 10^{-6})(2.0 \times 10^{-6})}{(0.30)^2} = 0.599\,\text{N},$$ pushing in the $-x$ direction.
From the charge on the $y$-axis: $$F_2 = (8.99 \times 10^{9})\dfrac{(4.0 \times 10^{-6})(2.0 \times 10^{-6})}{(0.40)^2} = 0.450\,\text{N},$$ pushing in the $-y$ direction.

Adding the sizes of forces that point in different directions. In the second example, $0.599 + 0.450 = 1.05\,\text{N}$ is wrong; the forces are at right angles, so the net is $0.749\,\text{N}$. Even on a line, a force pointing left must be subtracted. Check: the net force can never be bigger than the sum of the sizes, and equals that sum only when all the forces point the same way.
